content: 1. Among 101 participants, 39% (39/101) initiated an INSTI-based antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimen or added an INSTI to their existing ART regimen. The median gestational age (GA) at the time of ART intervention was 29 weeks, with a median GA of 33 weeks in the INSTI group and 27 weeks in the non-INSTI group. 2. Of the 39 INSTI regimens, four included dolutegravir (DTG) 50 mg once daily. Two participants started on a DTG regimen, one switched to DTG, and one intensified their regimen with DTG. All these interventions occurred between 33 and 36 weeks of gestation. 3. In a cohort of 90 women with baseline RNA levels allowing for a 1-log reduction, the median time to achieve a 1-log RNA decrease was 8 days (IQR 7–14) in the INSTI group compared to 35 days (IQR 20–53) in the non-INSTI group. A restricted sub-analysis showed similar results, with a median of 7 days for the INSTI group versus 11 days for the non-INSTI group. All women receiving DTG achieved a >1-log reduction in viral load (VL). 4. Maternal pharmacokinetics (PK) of DTG during pregnancy revealed that at 35 weeks of gestation, the maternal steady-state total and unbound DTG concentrations (C24) were 3007 ng/mL and 44 ng/mL, respectively. At day 9 of neonatal age, total and unbound DTG levels were 428 ng/mL and <10 ng/mL, respectively. By day 18, total DTG levels were <10 ng/mL, indicating complete elimination. The calculated terminal half-life of DTG in a two-phase model was 68 hours (initial phase) and 40 hours (terminal phase). Using this model, DTG levels in cord blood at delivery were predicted to be 4051 ng/mL. 5. The half-life of DTG was approximately four times longer in preterm infants compared to adults. This prolonged half-life, combined with the last measured maternal C24 of 3007 ng/mL two days before delivery, suggests potential accumulation of DTG in the fetal compartment. This finding indicates unexpected placental transfer of DTG, with fetal accumulation and slow neonatal clearance. 6. The mother in this case was also on atazanavir (ATV), which can increase the half-life of DTG by inhibiting UGT1A1 and CYP3A4. In healthy adults, ATV increases DTG trough levels by 121% and doubles the half-life to 24 hours. Additionally, ATV is a placental P-glycoprotein transporter inhibitor, which could limit fetal efflux of DTG. 7. Data from clinical trials and post-marketing reports included 263 pregnancy outcomes (42 from clinical trials and 221 from post-marketing data). Among these, 139 exposures had known trimesters: 116 in the first trimester, 12 in the second trimester, and 11 in the third trimester. Birth defects were categorized by organ system, with 16 defects reported in the first trimester, including central nervous system (CNS), cardiac, renal, musculoskeletal, genetic, and other anomalies. 8. Specific first-trimester defects included one neural tube defect (CNS), two cardiac defects (double-outlet right ventricle with ventricular septal defect [VSD] and patent ductus arteriosus [PDA]), and two renal defects (pelvi-ureteric obstruction and congenital hydronephrosis). Other anomalies included facial dysmorphy and unspecified defects. 9. Secondand third-trimester exposures were associated with nine defects, including renal anomalies (bilateral hydroureter, right hydronephrosis, renal dysplasia, and congenital renal cysts), musculoskeletal anomalies (polydactyly and syndactyly), and genetic anomalies (Down syndrome). Other reported outcomes included gestational sac without a fetal heart and abnormal auditory evoked potentials. 10. Data from the WHO VigiAccess database reported 2095 records of DTG exposure, including 57 pregnancy conditions and 32 congenital defect reports. No CNS defects were reported. Cardiac defects included anomalous pulmonary venous connection, atrial septal defect (ASD), and VSD. Renal defects included ectopic kidney, congenital hydronephrosis, renal hypoplasia, and congenital renal cysts. Musculoskeletal defects included polydactyly and syndactyly. Other anomalies included esophageal atresia, cystic fibrosis, trisomy 21, and congenital skin dimples. 11. For the combination therapy Triumeq (DTG/ABC/3TC), 2237 records included 27 pregnancy conditions and 15 congenital defect reports. Cardiac defects were the most common, including PDA, congenital heart disease, ASD, and VSD. Renal anomalies included congenital pyelocaliectasis and double ureter. Musculoskeletal anomalies included congenital pseudarthrosis. Other anomalies included cystic lymphangioma and dysmorphism. 12. Overall, the data suggest a potential association between DTG exposure during pregnancy and specific congenital anomalies, particularly cardiac and renal defects. However, the findings are limited by the lack of denominators and potential overlap between reporting mechanisms. Further research is needed to clarify these associations and assess the safety of DTG in pregnancy.
